title: Digital detoxing: When was the last time you took time off your screens?
summary: Fast-paced media has changed the way we live

blocks.text: There was a time when I realized that I had become more unfocused and forgetful. Whether it’s misplacing my phone or wallet, or needing to take multiple breaks during work, these issues all started occurring more frequently.

I took a step back to understand what had changed. But in fact, nothing changed; I connected my scattered attention to the time I spent on screens and realized what felt like harmless scrolling was starting to spill over into my everyday life.

Doomscrolling in the afternoon or watching movies while eating never seemed like a problem. Still, looking back, it seems like everything that I did always had a digital or auditory companion. Otherwise, every task would feel long, boring, or exhausting. That dependence made me reflect on how my screen time is starting to catch up with me mentally.

This research paper on social media’s impact on the human attention span, published earlier this year, describes my lack of focus and forgetfulness as a result of regular consumption of short-form content. The study suggests that my brain has been wired to feel rewarded by a simple scroll, making activities that require sustained attention feel unrewarding. This becomes problematic when the behavior becomes repetitive, and we begin to use doomscrolling as a way to regulate emotions. Moreover, short-form content was also shown to increase my potential risks of impulsivity, addiction-like behaviors, and depressive symptoms.

Realizing how attached I’ve become to my screen and how it has affected me mentally, I decided to make a change by making two simple promises to refocus and slow down: reduce my screen time by planning my day, and stick to the plan.

Going through a digital detox was one of the most life turning points for me as it shaped a lot of my interests and who I am today. Beyond reducing my time online, it became an act of getting to know myself and finding the right balance of being online and offline.

Finding this balance was the goal of my detox; it involved considering what I did throughout the day and making sure it was a healthy balance I could stick to. I knew simply reducing my screen time wouldn’t work, so I made small daily commitments to activities that would replace my time online.

My first commitment was to take time for physical activity, whether it was a short walk, a run, or a workout; it was my first non-negotiable to do for at least an hour a day. As someone who is already active, I knew it was something I could start with rather than trying to change my entire routine all at once. At first, it was a tiring conscious adjustment I had to keep in mind: tracking my online time and figuring out when and what activity to do. It was a challenging start, but after doing it consistently for a while, it became something that didn’t feel out of the ordinary.

I continued stacking up these commitments, ones that I knew I would enjoy and stick to, such as reading even just a page a day, drawing a simple sketch, learning a new song on the guitar or piano, and taking a short meditation in the morning. They all followed the same strategy: start small, do it every day until it becomes part of the routine, and repeat to the next commitment.

With relationships and work to consider, I knew some days would be too busy for me to follow through on all my commitments, and I allowed myself that flexibility. Detoxing wasn’t a prison I put myself in; it was a way to make room for things that mattered to me, and my relationships and work are part of those. That meant adjusting my commitments around my responsibilities and energy; even if I could only manage a few minutes of an activity or had to skip it for the day, it was all okay. After all, detoxing was an act of self-care for me.

Even though I started this detox a while back, I still find myself sticking to the habits I built. It was a life-changing experience as it taught me how to find a balance between staying connected online and making meaningful time for myself offline. That balance looks different each day, but what mattered to me was being more intentional and mindful about how I spend my time.

Digital detoxing is not a “fix” that could work for everyone. It’s a highly personal journey that you need to commit to that can bring some benefits to your life. What it has done for me is that I have become more mindful of the way I spend my time every day, taught me how to manage my mental health, and most importantly taught me a lot about who I am.

You don’t have to wait until you see signs of excessive digital consumption, as I did. Give it a try, starting with one small, screen-free break in your day. Spend that time doing something you enjoy, and notice how you feel afterward. From there, you can decide which boundaries fit your responsibilities and which habits are worth keeping. – Rappler.com

Masri-zada, T., Martirosyan, S., Abdou, A., Barbar, R., Kades, S., Makki, H., Haley, G., & Agrawal, D. K. (2018). The Impact of Social Media & Technology on Child and Adolescent Mental Health. J Psychiatry Psychiatr Disord. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12165459/
